content: Periodontal curettes are specialized dental instruments designed for the prophylactic and periodontal treatment of human teeth. The working tips of these instruments are available in various shapes and sizes, but they are always rounded at the tip. This rounded design minimizes trauma to the gingiva during subgingival cleaning. Due to this difference, curettes are the preferred instrument for addressing subgingival calculus deposits. For optimal use, the terminal shank of the curette, which is the portion of the handle closest to the blade, should be held parallel to the long axis of the tooth. To enhance their functionality, many curettes are designed with posterior analogs that feature angled terminal shanks, allowing for better access to posterior teeth. There are two primary categories of periodontal curettes: universal curettes and Gracey curettes. Universal curettes have blades that are positioned perpendicular to their terminal shanks. This configuration allows the blades to cut on both sides, making them effective for use on both the mesial and distal surfaces of teeth. The term universal reflects their versatility. These instruments are also known as Columbia curettes, as they were originally developed at the Columbia University College of Dental Medicine. Gracey curettes, on the other hand, have blades that are offset laterally by 70 degrees relative to the shank. This design results in a lower cutting edge and an upper non-cutting edge. Because only one side of the blade is functional, Gracey curettes are site-specific. For example, a Gracey curette designed for cleaning the mesial surfaces of posterior teeth cannot be used on the distal surfaces of those teeth. Similarly, a Gracey curette intended for the mesial surfaces of anterior teeth from the facial aspect can only be used on the distal surfaces of the same teeth when accessed from the lingual aspect.
